transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you so much for seeing me. Um, I guess... I'm here because I've been having a little trouble staying on task? It's probably nothing major, everyone gets distracted sometimes, but I just get pulled off track so easily. 

Like, if I'm working on a dashboard for a school project, just one little Slack ping, or even a song lyric playing in the background, or... or a random idea for another project pops into my head, and suddenly I've completely lost the thread of what I was supposed to be finishing. 

I hope that makes sense? Is that the right kind of thing to start with?
How long have you been experiencing this difficulty with staying on task? Has this always been a pattern for you, or is this something that started more recently?

Um, well... I guess I've always been a little bit of a daydreamer? But it really wasn't a big deal when I was younger. I'd say it only started causing, like, real problems for me about a year and five months ago? 

I hope it's okay that I know the exact timeframe, it's just... that's when things really shifted for me. I moved away from having super structured school projects and started trying to build my own freelance UX and data-visualization portfolio. Without a teacher giving me strict rubrics and deadlines, I just... I don't know, I guess I haven't been as disciplined as I should be. It's probably my own fault for not managing my time better, but yeah, it's been about a year and five months of really struggling with it. 

Is that the kind of timeline you were asking for?

Besides the work on your portfolio, have you noticed similar difficulties with staying focused or completing tasks in other areas of your life — like household chores, reading, conversations with friends, or other activities — or is this mainly happening when you're working on your freelance projects?

Um, well... I try really hard to keep on top of my chores and things, so I don't want to sound like I'm just completely disorganized all the time. But... I guess I do notice it a little bit with learning things? 

Like, if I sit down to read a research article, or even just watch a normal UX tutorial... I'll be looking right at it, but after a few minutes I'll realize my eyes have just been moving across the page or the screen, and I have absolutely no idea what I just took in. It's a little embarrassing to admit. I always go back and re-read it, of course, so I get it done eventually! But my brain just sort of... checks out for a minute, even when I really want to learn the material. 

Does that answer your question? I hope I'm giving you the right kind of information.

When you're trying to focus on something, do you find yourself feeling restless or fidgety, like you need to get up and move around? Or do you feel more like your energy is low and you're just mentally sluggish?

Um, I wouldn't really say I feel sluggish. I actually kind of have the opposite problem? I hope it doesn't make me sound like a bad student, but I guess I do get a little bit restless. 

I try really hard to be polite and sit still, especially if I have to sit through a long Zoom call for a class or just work quietly in one place. But after a while, I start feeling this... I don't know, this sort of uncomfortable pressure in my body? It just feels like I really need to get up and pace around, or at least do something with my hands. 

I usually try to hide it, like just doodling or playing with a pen off-camera so I'm not being disrespectful or distracting anyone else! It's probably just me having a little too much pent-up energy, but... yeah. Does that make sense? I hope I'm answering your question right.

When you're trying to focus on something, do you find yourself worrying a lot or feeling anxious about things — like worrying about whether you're doing well enough, or feeling nervous about the future — or is it more that external distractions and your restless energy are what pull your attention away?

Um, well... I don't think it's really anxiety? I mean, I care a lot about doing a good job, obviously, but I don't sit there worrying or feeling nervous about the future. It's more... um, the second thing you said. The distractions. 

Honestly, that's kind of the main reason I decided I should probably talk to someone. I just... I get pulled off track so easily. And I know I shouldn't, I really try to stay focused, but... like, if I get a Slack ping, or if I hear a specific song lyric, or even if I just get a random idea for a totally different project... suddenly I've just completely lost the thread of the dashboard I was supposed to be finishing. 

I feel awful when it happens, because I know I need to be more disciplined. It's just so easy for my brain to latch onto whatever else is happening around me. I hope that doesn't make me sound like I'm just not trying hard enough? Is that the kind of distraction you were asking about?

Around the time this started — about a year and five months ago when you moved to freelance work — did you notice any changes in your mood? Like, did you feel more sad, hopeless, or down than usual during that period, or has your mood stayed pretty consistent?

Um, no, I wouldn't say I felt sad or hopeless. I mean, I was actually really excited about starting freelance work! I felt really lucky to have the opportunity. 

My mood has been pretty normal, I think. I definitely haven't felt down or depressed or anything like that. I just... I get a little frustrated with myself sometimes when I can't stay on task, like I mentioned, but that's just because I want to do a good job, you know? It's not like a deep sadness. 

I try to keep a really positive attitude about everything. I hope that's a good thing? I just wouldn't want you to think I'm depressed when I'm really just struggling a bit with my focus. Does that make sense?

You mentioned you were always a bit of a daydreamer when you were younger. Back in elementary school or middle school, did teachers ever comment on you having trouble paying attention in class, or did you struggle to complete assignments even with the structure and deadlines they provided?

Um, well... I guess maybe they did a little bit? I really don't want to sound like I was a troublemaker or a bad kid, because I always respected my teachers and wanted them to like me! 

But, um, looking back at my elementary school report cards, they did sometimes write comments about me... like, rushing through my worksheets a bit too fast. And I guess I would sometimes lose track of the directions they gave us. They also mentioned a few times that I would talk over my classmates during group work... but I swear I wasn't trying to be rude! I think I was just really enthusiastic and eager to participate, you know? 

And with assignments at home... my parents actually used to sit right beside me while I did my homework. I think I just had a bad habit of wandering off or starting a completely different activity before I actually finished my math or reading. They were really sweet and supportive to sit there and help keep me on track, though. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound too awful? I really always tried my best to be a good student, my brain just wanted to do a hundred things at once back then. Does that answer your question okay?

When you think back to elementary school — say, around ages 6 to 12 — would you say that difficulty with attention and staying on task was pretty much a constant thing for you back then, or did it come and go?

Um, yeah, I guess it was pretty much a constant thing back then. I mean, I really hope I'm not repeating myself too much, but like I mentioned, my teachers were always writing those little notes on my report cards about me rushing through my worksheets or, um, losing track of the directions. And the talking over classmates thing during group work... that happened a lot, too. 

And at home, it was pretty much an everyday thing that my parents had to sit right there with me while I did my homework. If they didn't, I would just kind of... wander off to go play with something else or start drawing instead of finishing my assignments. It wasn't just once in a while, it was kind of how I always was. 

I really hope that doesn't make me sound like I was a nightmare child! I promise I was generally a happy, well-behaved kid, I just... I guess I've always just had a lot of energy and a wandering mind. Is it okay that it was happening that early on?

When you were in elementary school, did you have these same kinds of difficulties — trouble paying attention, getting distracted easily, having trouble finishing tasks — in multiple places, like both at school and at home, or was it mainly just in one setting?

Um, yeah, I guess it was happening in both places. Like I said, the teachers noticed it at school, and my parents definitely had to help me stay on track at home. 

But I really want to make sure you know that it wasn't like I was causing trouble everywhere I went! I feel like I'm making it sound like I was this chaotic kid, but I was just... easily sidetracked, I guess? Like, at home, I wasn't throwing tantrums or refusing to do my work. I just needed my mom or dad to gently remind me to finish my math problems instead of playing with my erasers. And at school, I was always polite to the teachers, even if I accidentally talked out of turn sometimes.

So, yes, it was at school and at home, but I really tried my best in both places. I hope that's what you were asking? I just don't want you to think I was a bad kid.

When you were in elementary school, besides the trouble focusing and getting distracted, did you also have a lot of trouble sitting still? Like, did teachers or your parents notice you were always running around, climbing on things, or fidgeting a lot — or was it mainly just the attention and focus issues?

Um, well... I don't think I was running around or climbing on things like a little terror or anything! I really tried to stay in my seat when I was supposed to. I was a good girl, I promise. 

But I guess... maybe I did fidget a bit? Even now, actually, if I have to sit still through a long Zoom call for my college classes, or if I have to just quietly work in one place for too long... I start feeling this sort of, um, uncomfortable pressure inside my body? It's hard to explain, but it's like I just really need to get up and pace around, or at least do something with my hands. 

I try really hard to hide it, though! I don't want to be disruptive or make anyone think I'm not paying attention to them. I usually just bounce my leg under the desk where no one can see, or fiddle with a pen. Does that make sense? I hope that doesn't make me sound too antsy or impatient!

When you were in elementary school, do you remember your parents or teachers saying that you had a lot of energy and were always on the go — like, did they ever describe you as being 'hyper' or say that you were always running around and hard to keep up with?

Um, well, I don't think they ever used the word "hyper" like... like I was bouncing off the walls or anything bad like that. I was pretty well-behaved! But, um, I guess I have always liked to stay busy? 

Even now, like on days when I don't have college classes or a real schedule, I still kind of... jump around a lot. Like I'll go from editing a design prototype to suddenly deciding I need to clean my desk, and then I'll open up a new dataset for a project. It's just that, um, resting kind of feels weird to me unless I'm actively doing something? 

I just like being productive, I guess! I really hope that's okay, and that it doesn't sound like I'm too scattered or anything. I just try to make the most of my time, you know? Is that the kind of thing you mean?

target_item.manifestation: On days when I don’t have classes or a formal schedule, I still jump from editing a prototype to cleaning my desk to opening a new dataset, like resting feels weird unless I’m actively doing something.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I was described as having a lot of energy, being 'hyper', or 'always on the go', which directly maps to the symptom of acting as if 'driven by a motor' or constant activity.

patient.answer:
Um, well, I don't think they ever used the word "hyper" like... like I was bouncing off the walls or anything bad like that. I was pretty well-behaved! But, um, I guess I have always liked to stay busy? 

Even now, like on days when I don't have college classes or a real schedule, I still kind of... jump around a lot. Like I'll go from editing a design prototype to suddenly deciding I need to clean my desk, and then I'll open up a new dataset for a project. It's just that, um, resting kind of feels weird to me unless I'm actively doing something? 

I just like being productive, I guess! I really hope that's okay, and that it doesn't sound like I'm too scattered or anything. I just try to make the most of my time, you know? Is that the kind of thing you mean?

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the chief complaint that brings the patient to the clinic
opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with persistent inattention (difficulty maintaining focus on tasks, easily distracted by external stimuli and internal thoughts), hyperactivity-impulsivity (restlessness, fidgeting, difficulty remaining seated, constant need for activity), and impulsivity (rushing through work, interrupting peers). Symptoms began in elementary school (ages 6-12) as a constant pattern, persist across multiple settings (school and home historically; now college and work), and continue into adulthood. Recent exacerbation coincides with reduced external structure. While current functional impairment is primarily occupational (portfolio work), the lifelong pattern and childhood onset are consistent with ADHD, Combined Presentation. F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified) is assigned due to insufficient clarity on current symptom distribution across inattention vs. hyperactivity-impulsivity domains; F90.0 (Predominantly Inattentive Type) remains a strong alternative given the emphasis on attentional difficulties.
